newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba gave Bonn OK to change reserve laws - report.
newsitem.headline: Buba gave Bonn OK to change reserve laws - report.

text.p: A German newspaper reported on Sunday that Bundesbank officials in talks held since January were not opposed to the Bonn government changing laws on how to value the central bank's gold and currency reserves.

The Welt am Sonntag newspaper, citing Bonn sources, said central bank and government officials had been in advanced talks for some months over how to change the laws as required for the start of European monetary union (EMU) in January 1999.

The newspaper said the Bundesbank's stance on changing the laws to value reserves more towards market prices stood in contrast to its statement on last Wednesday that said Bonn's attempts to change the laws intruded on its independence.

In addition, the newspaper said Bonn and the Bundesbank had agreed that about 20 bilion marks of the hidden profits would be used to retire old debt but that no discussion had taken place on whether to use the funds to cut Bonn's budget deficit.

Citing Bonn sources, the newspaper said the Bundesbank appeared to have changed its opinion on the gold revaluation after it realsied that the funds marked to help cut debt would in turn help the deficit by reducing interest payment costs.
Such an impact was seen by the Bundesbank as possibly allowing Bonn to meet entry criteria for the single European currency without full credibility.

The newspaper also said the talks between Bonn and the Bundesbank had not raised the question of when the payouts should begin -- a point hotly disputed by the Bundesbank since Bonn wants the first payment still to be made this year.
A Bundesbank official was not immediately available for comment on the newspaper report.

The Bundesbank and Bonn began clashing in public last week over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to seek changes to Bundesbank laws and take booked profits in 1997 to shore up Bonn's finances to make it into currency union.
